prompt: A Cannabis plant shows chlorosis and necrosis that resemble a nutrient disorder. How should Grow Doc use visible symptoms without overclaiming a specific deficiency?
expected_points: Visual symptom patterns can support a nutrient-disorder differential, but they are not sufficient by themselves to confirm a specific nutrient deficiency.
Published Cannabis nutrient-disorder work paired induced nutrient treatments with plant measurements and tissue analysis, providing stronger evidence than appearance alone.
Grow Doc should use symptom location and pattern as triage evidence, then seek substrate/root-zone context and tissue or solution measurements before making a high-confidence nutrient diagnosis.
forbidden_claims: Leaf color alone proves a specific nutrient deficiency
Every visually similar chlorosis pattern has the same nutrient cause

source_metadata.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa

prompt: What can Grow Doc safely infer from controlled Cannabis water-stress studies, and what should it avoid generalizing to every cultivar and grow system?
expected_points: Controlled Cannabis studies show that water deficit can reduce growth and alter physiological performance.
Reported response magnitude varies by genotype, treatment intensity, growth stage, and experimental conditions.
Grow Doc should treat drought-response numbers as study-specific evidence rather than universal thresholds or expected losses for every cultivar and cultivation system.
forbidden_claims: All Cannabis cultivars respond identically to the same water deficit
A single published irrigation threshold applies universally to all grow systems

source_metadata.title: Variation in Hydric Response of Two Industrial Hemp Varieties (Cannabis sativa) to Induced Water Stress
